messages:
maria: Quick check — we're deciding between protobuf-first gRPC internal surfaces vs JSON/REST for the new routing/quotas controlplane. Main concerns: console UX for rollouts, telemetry granularity (sampling vs full traces), and how easy it is for platform teams to do canary routing. thoughts?

sam: +1 for listing tradeoffs. my gut: gRPC + proto gives typed contracts and smaller payloads (good for high qps), but it makes browser-based console integrations slightly harder. :thinking: 

li: We should ask: who is the primary client? platform services (machine) or console (browser/human)? if mostly services -> proto. if console needs direct calls -> rest or a gateway/transcode.

maria: Primarily services for runtime routing decisions, but console needs realtime-ish info (rollout state, signals) and quick ad-hoc checks. we prefer a single source of truth instead of two diverging APIs.

devin: What about hybrid: proto for internal machine-to-machine and a small REST fronting gateway for console + integrations. Gateway could do on-the-fly transcoding and add helpful fields (human-readable enums).

kevin: Hybrid seems pragmatic. caveat: gateway adds operational surface and latency. we need clear SLAs and automated tests to ensure parity. also quotas header propagation is annoying across translation. e.g., we rely on `X-Redwood-Route` + tenant headers — gateway must preserve them.

anika: UX note: console rollout controls benefit from websockets/streaming for live signals (progress, error spikes). gRPC streaming fits nicely, but browsers need gRPC-web or a WS shim. Converting streams to SSE/WS at the gateway works.

maria: telemetry question — do we sample on ingress and propagate trace IDs? or should the controlplane add its own sampling to keep storage sane?

sam: Keep an ingress sampling decision and carry trace IDs. controlplane can enrich events with rollout metadata and do downstream sampling for high-volume routes. 

li: For metrics/alerts we need per-route histograms (p50/p95/p99 latency) and per-tenant quota counters. If using proto, include route id in every RPC header so telemetry and billing can tag easily. Example header: `X-Route-Id: r_abc123` and `X-Tenant: t_456`

devin: Implementation detail: if we do proto-first, design proto messages to be forward-compatible (optional fields, oneof) and publish them in a shared repo. automate generation of server/client libs in go/ts. 

kevin: Ops concern: migration strategy. We should support a dual-stack for a while and have a traffic split controlled by routing policy. console can default to REST gateway, services to proto. Rollout plan: 0 -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% with canary checks for telemetry drift.

anika: For canary signals, console should display both modelled and observed metrics. We want to show delta in request latency and error rate plus quota burn. Small mock: `CanarySignal { route, pct, p95_before, p95_after, quota_delta }`

maria: One practical hitch: SDKs. We have internal go/java/node SDKs that expect JSON shapes today. shifting to proto could break teams. how invasive will regen be?

sam: If we generate idiomatic clients and keep a thin JSON wrapper on top of proto for higher-level SDK functions, migration can be gradual. also add feature flags to keep old endpoints.

ops-bot: deploy-bot: Canaries are available in staging. runbook link: https://go/redwood/runbooks/canary-checklist :white_check_mark:

li: Last thought — prefer proto-first for runtime paths, with a small, well-tested REST gateway for human-facing flows and third-party integrations. ensure header propagation and streaming shims are first-class.

maria: OK that's the leaning here. i'll draft an RFC that outlines hybrid architecture, header contract (`X-Route-Id`, `X-Tenant`, `X-Redwood-Sampling`), migration steps, and telemetry sampling rules. tagging @dev-ex for SDK impact. thanks all :raised_hands:
